raw.assessment: The incumbent assembles reversible partitions and checks the order before packing, plausibly providing a contents check and an initial layout reference. Its effectiveness is limited: median time is 11 minutes, five reports concern partitions, and only seven of ten observed customers arranged theirs unaided. Reports do not establish five verified packing errors. Repeated three-compartment orders taking seven to nine minutes are a concrete counterexample to uniformly slow work; mixed batches contain every extreme delay, but layout complexity and switching remain confounded. Overlapping widths also limit a width-only explanation of insertion retries. These observations do not establish pilot success.

openings.claim: Changing layouts between orders adds selection or checking work beyond the intrinsic assembly cost of complex layouts.
openings.delta: Separates transition overhead from compartment-count difficulty before changing production sequencing.
openings.prediction: For the same layout and worker, orders following a different layout take longer chiefly during selection or checking; intrinsic complexity instead persists within repeated-layout runs.
openings.probe: Reuse twelve sample organizers across blocked and alternating sequences containing equal layout counts. Counterbalance sequence order between workers, balance exterior colors, and separately time selection, insertion, checking and packing. Record content errors and insertion retries.
assumptions: Sample parts tolerate reuse without changing fit; track wear.
Bench time fits the fixed delivery schedule; accepted configurations remain intact.

openings.claim: For complete kits, the generic three-layout diagram leaves the short partition's position ambiguous; an order-specific placement map could improve unaided arrangement.
openings.delta: Tests an information cause independently of actual missing or incorrect parts.
openings.prediction: With verified correct contents, customers given the placement map make fewer short-partition placement errors and requests for help.
openings.probe: Randomly assign ten participants, balanced by layout, to the current diagram or an order-specific map. Observe first unpacking, unaided success within ten minutes, placement errors and help requests. Treat this small comparison as directional; measure map preparation time and cost before adoption.
assumptions: Maps depict existing reversible parts, selected counts and colors within the current footprint and capacity.
Implementation stays within 500 initial and 0.40 recurring cost, available labor and the fixed date.

raw.assessment: One interaction hypothesis merits a bounded test. Missing-part reports and short-partition confusion suggest a shared identification interface, but neither their causes nor savings from changing it are established. Combined assembly/packing timing cannot identify the bottleneck.

openings.claim: Cross a reusable order-specific component staging mat with an ordered-layout diagram through shared part-to-position keys at the packing-to-unpacking interface. Each required partition occupies a keyed outline during checking; the same key appears beside its destination on the replacement diagram and on a removable paper sleeve around that partition. The hypothesis is that verified component identity carried into placement guidance improves successful customer arrangement beyond either checking or guidance alone.
openings.delta: The mat alone can check a kit without explaining placement; the diagram alone can explain placement without establishing that its depicted parts were supplied. Their shared keys let customers connect checked physical parts to intended positions, especially the short partition. Stage components for checking, then preserve the existing assembled delivery format; sleeves must remain readable on unpacking and removable for rearrangement.
openings.prediction: If the interaction matters, combining both mechanisms will improve unaided ordered-layout completion more than the sum of their separate improvements over the incumbent, while reducing short-partition identification errors. Extra handling may instead erase any workshop time benefit.
openings.probe: Use 12 of the 15 sample units across four conditions: incumbent, mat only, keyed diagram/sleeves only, and both. Balance workers and layout complexity; record selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, and audit actual contents against each order. Randomly allocate the ten customers to one first-use condition each; record unaided completion and misplaced short partitions. Treat this small experiment as screening, not proof of interaction or pilot thresholds. Measure sleeve/material cost and preparation time before use on accepted orders.
assumptions: Keys distinguish otherwise confusable partitions and transfer without packing mistakes.
Sleeves do not obstruct seating, alter capacity or damage surfaces.
Initial cost stays within 500 and recurring material increase within 0.40 per order; this is unverified.

Retain footprint, stationery capacity, removable partitions, ordered compartment counts, exterior colors and fixed delivery date. Stop adoption if preparation threatens the date; validate the stated success measures in the 60-unit pilot.

openings.claim: Layout switching adds selection/checking overhead beyond complexity.
openings.discriminator: Same-layout times rise after transitions; intrinsic complexity persists in repeats.
openings.probe: Counterbalance blocked/alternating sequences using 12 reusable samples; balance workers, layouts, colors; time four stages, audit contents and retries.
openings.uncertainty: Switching and complexity are confounded; monitor reuse wear.

openings.claim: Order-specific maps resolve short-partition ambiguity in verified complete kits.
openings.discriminator: Fewer placement errors/help requests with correct contents held constant.
openings.probe: Randomize ten first-use customers, balancing layouts, between current diagram and map; measure unaided ten-minute completion, errors, help and preparation cost/time.
openings.uncertainty: Reports do not establish packing errors; small comparison is directional.

openings.claim: Shared keys on staging mat, layout diagram and removable partition sleeves connect verified identity to placement.
openings.discriminator: Combined benefit exceeds summed separate benefits.
openings.probe: Screen incumbent, mat, diagram/sleeves and both across 12 samples; balance workers/layouts, audit contents, time stages; allocate ten first-use customers across conditions.
openings.uncertainty: Small groups cannot prove interaction; extra handling, key transfer, sleeve seating/capacity/surface effects and costs remain unverified.

post_distill.decision: Prioritize D1 and D2; D3 competes for the same ten first-use participants. Keep assembled delivery, 30x20 footprint, capacity, reversible partitions, ordered counts/colors and fixed date; verify <=500 initial and <=0.40 recurring cost. Screen within 15 samples; adoption requires the 60-unit pilot: >=98% complete, median <=8 minutes, >=90% unaided. No success established.
